---
title: "Quiz: finding objects as boxes"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Two $8 \times 8$ boxes overlap in a $4 \times 8$ strip. What is their IoU?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Union = area A + area B − intersection.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Intersection 32, union $64 + 64 - 32 = 96$, IoU $= 1/3$.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does a detector produce several boxes for one object?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many grid positions look at the same object?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every grid position near the object sees it and proposes a box for it (how the grid guesses: the next day, [single-shot detection](../yolo/lec.qmd)). Neighbouring positions give similar, overlapping boxes: duplicates that must be removed.
:::

---

**Q3.** In greedy NMS with threshold $t$, what happens if $t$ is too low? Too high?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$t$ is the overlap above which a box is deleted.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Too low: boxes of true neighbouring objects overlap the kept box by more than $t$ and are deleted (missed objects). Too high: duplicates of the same object overlap by less than $t$ and survive (false positives).
:::

---

**Q4.** A small spot of $3 \times 3$ pixels is detected with a box shifted by one pixel. Is it a TP at IoU $\ge 0.5$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Intersection $2 \times 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Intersection 6, union $9 + 9 - 6 = 12$, IoU 0.5: just at the threshold. Shifted in both directions: $4/14 = 0.29$, a miss. IoU thresholds are very strict for small objects.
:::

---

**Q5.** AP is high but F1 is low. What does that tell you about the detections?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
AP depends on the ranking, F1 on the boxes above a threshold.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The true detections have the highest scores (good ranking), but many low-scored false boxes (e.g. surviving duplicates) are kept at the chosen operating point. A higher score threshold or a lower NMS threshold would raise F1.
:::

---

**Q6.** *(math)* Show that $1 - \mathrm{IoU}$ gives no gradient for two boxes that do not overlap.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the intersection for small shifts?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If the boxes do not overlap, the intersection is 0 and stays 0 for any small shift, so $\mathrm{IoU} = 0$ and $1 - \mathrm{IoU} = 1$ in a whole neighbourhood: the derivative is zero.
:::

---

**Q7.** Name the three meanings of "non-maximum suppression" in this course.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Edges, accumulators, boxes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Canny (keep gradient values that are maximal across the edge), peak picking (keep local maxima of a Hough accumulator or heat map), and box NMS (delete boxes that overlap a better box by more than $t$). Polygon NMS (next day, StarDist) is the box rule with polygon IoU.
:::
